title: Knowledge Representation & Expert Systems
intro: Before machine learning became popular, AI meant writing expert knowledge down as clear rules. Those rules are still used today. Anyone can read them and check how a decision was reached.

sections.heading: 1. Symbolic AI: Smart Software Built on Clear Rules

analogy.description: When tax software helps you file a return, it does not guess. It follows a long list of rules, such as giving you a credit if you installed solar panels and own your home. You can always see why each figure appears.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Symbolic AI** is built on written knowledge: words, facts, and rules that experts have typed into the system.

The software does not study millions of examples to find hidden patterns. It simply follows the rules it was given. This makes its behavior predictable and easy to check, because the same input always gives the same answer.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: AI that follows written facts and rules instead of learning from data.
Gives the same answer every time for the same input.

diagram.caption: How a rule-based system reaches an answer
diagram.alt: A flow from left to right: a fact comes in, a matching if-then rule is found, the rule is applied, and the answer comes with the rule that produced it.
diagram.content:
flowchart LR
    A["Fact comes in"] --> B["Find matching rule"] --> C["Apply the rule"] --> D["Answer + the rule used"]

sections.realWorld: Tax software and loan-eligibility checkers that follow written rules.

sections.heading: 2. Inside an Expert System: Rules and a Reasoning Engine

analogy.description: In a hospital, the handbook of symptoms and diseases is kept separate from the nurse who sorts incoming patients. The handbook can be updated without retraining the nurse.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
In the 1970s and 1980s, researchers built **expert systems** to copy the way human specialists make decisions. Every expert system has two main parts:

1. **The knowledge base**, which is a store of facts and if-then rules written by experts.
2. **The inference engine**, which checks the facts against the rules, decides which rules apply, and draws a conclusion.

Because the two parts are kept separate, a doctor or engineer can update a rule without changing the software that runs it.

diagram.caption: Decoupled Architecture: Knowledge Base + Inference Engine
diagram.content:
graph TD Facts["📋 Working Memory
(Observed Symptoms / Inputs)"] --> Engine["⚙️ Inference Engine
(Pattern Matcher & Reasoner)"] KB["📚 Knowledge Base
(If-Then Production Rules)"] --> Engine Engine --> Output["✅ Verified Conclusion & Audit Trail"]
diagram.alt: Two inputs feed one engine. Observed inputs in working memory and if-then rules in the knowledge base go into the inference engine, which produces a conclusion with an audit trail.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: The collection of facts and if-then rules.
The part that applies the rules to the facts.
Start with known facts, fire the rules that match, and reach a conclusion.

sections.realWorld: Medical checklists and car-repair scanners that match symptoms to causes.

sections.heading: 3. Interactive Simulation: Forward Chaining Diagnostic Engine

analogy.description: When a mechanic plugs a scanner into your car, the car's computer checks its sensors and reports a likely reason why the check-engine light came on.

sections.bodyMarkdown: Try the simulator below by switching the sensor readings on and off. As you do, watch which rules match the readings and which conclusion appears at the end.

interactiveWidget.title: 🚀 Interactive Simulation: The Mars Rover Expert System
interactiveWidget.goal: Turn on the sensor readings that trigger the right diagnosis.
interactiveWidget.predictionPrompt: Before you change any input: which rule do you expect to match?
hints: Rules fire only when all their conditions are true.
Try one input at a time.
interactiveWidget.successMessage: That is forward chaining: facts go in, matching rules fire, and a conclusion comes out.

sections.realWorld: The check-engine light: sensors trigger rules that point to a fault.

miniQuiz.question: What is the primary advantage of decoupling the Knowledge Base from the Inference Engine?
options: Domain specialists can update rules without rewriting the core reasoning software
It makes the program run 100 times faster than compiled C code
It allows the computer to run without electricity
miniQuiz.praise: Excellent! Separating rules from reasoning allows experts to maintain the knowledge base independently.
miniQuiz.explanation: Decoupling ensures that domain knowledge can be maintained, verified, and expanded without touching the core engine algorithms.

miniQuiz.question: Which of the following best describes Forward Chaining?
options: Starting with known observations and applying rules forward to deduce conclusions
Guessing an outcome and working backward to justify it
Connecting physical computers together with networking cables
miniQuiz.praise: Exactly right! Forward chaining is data-driven reasoning moving from facts to conclusions.
miniQuiz.explanation: Forward chaining is a bottom-up, data-driven inference method that triggers matching rules until no further deductions can be made.

miniQuiz.question: Why is Symbolic AI still widely used in flight control and healthcare systems today?
options: Because it is 100% explainable, deterministic, and leaves a complete audit trail
Because neural networks are illegal in airplanes
Because modern computers cannot run machine learning models
miniQuiz.praise: Spot on! When human safety is on the line, having a verifiable audit trail of rules is indispensable.
miniQuiz.explanation: Symbolic rule-based logic is essential in mission-critical applications where every single automated decision must be provably verifiable.

teachBack.prompt: Which sentence best explains a rule-based system?
options: It applies written if-then rules, so each answer can be traced.
It learns hidden patterns from large data sets.
It predicts outcomes with probabilities and cannot explain them.
teachBack.explanation: Rule-based systems are transparent because every conclusion points to a rule.

recall.question: What is Narrow AI?
options: AI built to do one specific job well
AI that can do any job a person can
AI that only works on small computers
recall.explanation: All AI that exists today is Narrow AI.
